title: Heathrow Airport warns third runway could be delayed by four years
description: Heathrow Airport has warned that its planned third runway might be delayed by four years due to planning and regulatory issues.The government had hope
body: Heathrow Airport has warned that its planned third runway might be delayed by four years due to planning and regulatory issues.The government had hoped the new runway at the UK's busiest airport, estimated to cost £49bn, would open by 2035.But Heathrow sees this deadline as increasingly difficult to deliver without further steps to simplify the planning process. It said on Saturday that it hoped to secure planning permission by 2029 and then open the runway "within a decade".The Department for Transport (DfT) said the project's timeline had "always been ambitious" and that it would continue to work with stakeholders "at pace" on the matter.The airport said its "core scenario" had always been to open a new runway within a decade of securing planning permission.It said it was encouraged by the chancellor's efforts to streamline infrastructure and remove policy and regulatory bottlenecks, and promised to continue to work with ministers, airlines and stakeholders to "progress the planning application with pace".Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government's support for the project in January 2025, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham - who was previously critical - said he was "open-minded" about the scheme when he came to office.Despite attracting wide opposition from environmental campaigners and local resident groups from neighbouring areas, the project is expected to create around 100,000 jobs and provide a major boost to the economy.The expansion would mean demolishing hundreds of homes, diverting rivers, and rerouting the M25 motorway between junctions 14 and 15 through a tunnel under the new runway.The number of flights from the airport, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average.London Mayor Sadiq Khan has always opposed the project, warning of the impact on noise, air pollution and climate change.A draft of the planning framework for the expansion was published in June this year for consultation. Once finalised, it then needs to be put to a parliamentary vote, which could reportedly be delayed until 2027.A DfT spokesperson said: "There is currently no live planning application for a third runway, and we cannot comment on ongoing consultation processes or prejudice them in a way that will only delay progress."The timeline has always been ambitious. We'll continue to work with promoters, including Heathrow, and all other stakeholders at pace to ensure the right framework is in place for which a planning application for a third runway could be considered."A spokesperson for Heathrow said: "It's right that ambitious targets were set; the sooner expansion begins, the sooner the whole UK will benefit."They said the benefits would involve "at least 108,000 new jobs and billions of pounds invested in supply chains in every part of the country"."This is a national project, 100% privately financed which will support growth today and secure the UK's position in the global economy once the runway opens."Heathrow is the UK's busiest airport, serving more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways.

schema.headline: Heathrow Airport warns third runway could be delayed by four years

title: Huge crowds greet Pope in Paris ahead of open-air Mass
description: Figure caption, Watch: Huge crowds greeted the Pope as he travelled down the Champs-ÉlyséesByJacob PhillipsUpdated 2 hours agoHundreds of thousands of
body: Figure caption, Watch: Huge crowds greeted the Pope as he travelled down the Champs-ÉlyséesByJacob PhillipsUpdated 2 hours agoHundreds of thousands of people have greeted Pope Leo XIV in the centre of Paris for a giant open-air Mass.Crowds cheered as the pontiff moved down the Champs-Élysées Avenue beneath the Arc de Triomphe, waving to crowds from his popemobile.The head of the Catholic Church blessed several babies as he stopped at different stages along the avenue as chants of "Leo, Leo" rang out.More than half a million people are expected to attend the event in the heart of the French capital on Saturday and a special altar has been built on the Place de la Concorde for the ceremony.Image source, ReutersFrench President Emmanuel Macron, who met Leo for an hour of talks on Friday, will not be at any of the Pope's Masses during his four-day visit to France, largely to avoid breaching France's strict separation of state and religion.But the Champs-Élysées Mass will be attended by Macron's wife Brigitte and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu.Several candidates for next year's presidential election are also expected to attend.Marine Le Pen of the hard-right National Rally party and conservative Bruno Retailleau were both pictured at the Place de la Concorde ahead of the event, while centrists Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal are also due to be there.Mayor of Le Havre and former French Prime Minister Edouard Philippe and former Prime Minister Francois Fillon were both also seen at the Place de la Concorde.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Thousands have gathered along Champs-Elysees Avenue ahead of Pope Leo's open-air MassEarlier on Saturday, the Pope met migrants as he visited the Maison Bakhita centre, an association supporting refugees, and praised the organisation for inviting "us to see those who are invisible".During the visit Leo said it was "possible to encounter one another and to live together in dignity and peace".He also stressed the "the fundamental role of women in building a civilisation of love".The Pope also issued a warning about the dangers of artificial intelligence (AI) at the start of his visit to France on Friday.Leo cautioned against "losing our humanity amid a paradise of machines" in wide-ranging remarks to Church and state officials at the Élysée Palace.Image source, ReutersFigure caption, Why is the Pope in France?Large crowds are expected throughout the pontiff's trip, which the Church believes reflects a growing spirituality among the French and other Europeans.On Sunday, 150,000 have signed up to attend mass in the Pyrenean sanctuary of Lourdes.The Pope will be in Metz, in northeast France, on Monday where he will pay tribute to Robert Schuman (1886-1963), a founding father of the European Union and a fervent Catholic who is today a candidate for beatification.Born in Chicago in 1955, Pope Leo XIV was originally called Robert Prevost – a French name.His paternal grandmother was born in Le Havre in Normandy in 1894. When she married in the US many years later, she and her Italian husband took the name Prevost, which had been her mother's maiden name.

schema.headline: Huge crowds greet Pope in Paris ahead of open-air Mass

title: Met to re-examine CCTV footage from unsolved Jill Dando murder
description: The TV presenter and newsreader was born in Weston-Super-Mare, Somerset, and worked for the BBC for 14 years. She was 37 when she died on the doorstep
body: The TV presenter and newsreader was born in Weston-Super-Mare, Somerset, and worked for the BBC for 14 years. She was 37 when she died on the doorstep of her home on Gowan Avenue.Soon after her death, a man of Serbian descent called the BBC claiming she had been executed in a revenge hit for the UK-backed Nato bombing of Serbia's state broadcaster in Belgrade.However, Barry George, a local man, was convicted of her murder and spent eight years in jail before being acquitted at a retrial in 2008. Dando's partner, Alan Farthing, was interviewed by the police, along with her ex-partner and BBC Breakfast news editor Bob Wheaton. Also interviewed was her agent Jon Roseman, who had written a crime novel detailing a very similar scene.They were all ruled out as suspects. Her killing was the subject of a Netflix documentary Who Killed Jill Dando? in 2023.Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

schema.headline: Met to re-examine CCTV footage from unsolved Jill Dando murder

title: Athens explosion: Six dead in blast near Acropolis in Plaka district
description: Six people have died, including a British national, in an explosion that destroyed a building housing a holiday rental property in the historic centre
body: Six people have died, including a British national, in an explosion that destroyed a building housing a holiday rental property in the historic centre of Athens.The blast on Friday happened in the Plaka area of the Greek capital, a neighbourhood close to tourist sites such as the Acropolis.Four American holidaymakers were among the dead, along with a UK national and Greek national - reportedly an elderly couple who lived in the same building. Pictures from the scene on Saturday showed emergency service workers searching through rubble, with a gas leak the suspected cause of the blast.All six bodies had been recovered by Saturday afternoon. Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said: "We are talking about an incredible disaster."The tourists were confirmed to be missing when they did not arrive for their flight at Athens airport later on Friday, Reuters news agency reported citing local police.The three-storey building completely collapsed due to the force of the blast, with neighbouring buildings damaged and debris scattered across the road.

schema.headline: Athens explosion: Six dead in blast near Acropolis in Plaka district

title: Iran offers US deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz in seven days
description: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says his country has proposed a deal to the US that would see the Strait of Hormuz reopened within a week.Arag
body: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says his country has proposed a deal to the US that would see the Strait of Hormuz reopened within a week.Araghchi told reporters at the UN in New York that this could be done "if the necessary conditions are met" and said these were contained within the memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in June."The choice now rests with the United States," he said, adding the plan was delivered to the US via Qatar.Asked about the Iranian offer, a US official told the BBC positive discussions were taking place through mediators, including about nuclear issues. While the US has yet to deliver its official response to the proposal, the Wall Street Journal, citing US officials, reported that US President Donald Trump had rejected the deal., externalTrump was privately sceptical that Iran would meet his demands, it reported, and had told his staff that he saw a renewed bombing campaign as likely.The US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on 28 February. Iran responded by attacking Israel and US bases in the Gulf and Arab Gulf allies of the US - as well as blocking the Strait of Hormuz.Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to pass through the strait before the war and its closure has caused wild fluctuations of energy prices.It has also increased pressure on Trump to find a way of ending the conflict - particularly as the US heads to Congressional elections in November."If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, a normal maritime passage restored within seven days," Araghchi told reporters.He did not specify what steps Iran wanted the US to take but added that "the actions that the United States should take are not new. They are all already in the MOU". "I can tell you if there is seriousness in the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared," he added.A US official told the BBC that the US was "in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz, so we are not in a rush".In an interview with CBS News, the BBC's US partner, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that the ceasefire process "will begin from the very day they accept it"."We had previously reached an agreement based on the MOU that was signed in Pakistan... if the United States agrees to proceed in that way, everything will return to the way it was before," he added.Pezeshkian also said Iran would now allow UN nuclear inspectors into the country.Rejecting claims that Iran is trying to develop a nuclear weapon, the Iranian president said: "If they wish to come in and have inspections, we can reach accords and agreements vis-à-vis that specific topic within the negotiations."The MOU between the US and Iran, signed on 18 June, was designed to bring about a ceasefire and at least partly reopen the Strait of Hormuz. The 14-point agreement said Iran would never have a nuclear weapon. It noted that the US, Iran and their allies would end military operations on "all fronts" and contained provisions including the end of a US naval blockade and sanctions relief. It also said Iran would "make arrangements using its best efforts for the safe passage of commercial vessels" through the strait and hold talks with Oman over future shipping arrangements.But it fell apart a short time later when both sides resumed strikes.Iran has attacked vessels it says have attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz without authorisation.The US has attacked Iranian sites in the strait - as well as Iranian tankers off the country's coast. It has also maintained a blockade of Iranian ports, causing huge disruption to the Iranian economy.Trump since has claimed the US has been successful in getting oil out through the Strait of Hormuz. Shipping data shows a recent 10-day average of about 18 transits per day, with daily numbers dropping as low as nine vessels on certain days, according to Kpler, a commodities data and analytics firm cited by Reuters.However, Yemen's Houthis - allied to Iran - have recently intensified attacks aimed at disrupting oil exports from Saudi Arabia via the Red Sea on the other side of the Arabian peninsula.The group seized large strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive this month, including the port of Mokha, which overlooks the Bab al-Mandab Strait, another chokepoint for global shipping.The situation has been exacerbated by Houthi attacks on Saudi oil installations. US media has reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has requested military support from Trump.On Saturday, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said it had intercepted two ballistic missiles and drones launched by the Houthis towards Saudi Arabia.During his speech at the UN General Assembly this week, Trump said he believed an Iran deal, which has so far eluded him, would come right after November's elections."Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" he said."Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell?"On Friday, Araghchi said Iran did not accept "coercion, threats or intimidation" and added that "peace cannot be built through threats of annihilation".

schema.headline: Iran offers US deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz in seven days

title: Indonesia Carstensz Pyramid: Papua's 'eternal snow' on Puncak Jaya is about to disappear forever
description: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear foreverImage source, Project Pressure/Klaus ThymannImage caption, Only smal
body: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear foreverImage source, Project Pressure/Klaus ThymannImage caption, Only small patches of snow remain on Papua's Sudirman RangeByAbraham UtamaBBC IndonesiaThe mountains of Papua are not far from the equator, but they've been topped with "eternal snow" for centuries.The peaks in this Indonesian region on the world's second-largest island, just north of Australia, have offered scientists countless insights into the Earth's climate history.They're also the epicentre of the spiritual universe for many Papuans - a Mecca or a Vatican, as one activist puts it.But now, nearly all the snow is gone.A century ago, the 300km (190-mile) stretch of the Sudirman Range had snow and permanent ice on all four of its major peaks.But now there are only small areas around Puncak Jaya, also known as Carstensz Pyramid, with any snow at all. These are expected to entirely disappear in a year or two.Glacier cover around the peak has shrunk from nearly 1,900 hectares (4,700 acres) in the 19th Century to about 16 hectares (40 acres) today. Almost entire glaciers have vanished within a human lifetime."There is a profound unfairness in this," says Marie Šabacká, a Czech glacier ecologist who travelled to Puncak Jaya last March in a bid to be among the last scientists to study Papua's "eternal snow".She says the tropical glaciers in Papua are unique because they are separated from other glacier systems by thousands of kilometres. Papua is home to the "last remaining tropical ice" between the Andes and Himalayas.Ice cores taken from the slopes of Puncak Jaya preserve a record of climate history. Scientists can use them to obtain information about atmospheric conditions in the region and understand changes in the planet's warmest ocean waters that surround the island - the tropical Pacific and Western Pacific Warm pool.But this archive is disappearing before scientists have had time to fully study it.Image caption, The snow cover has reduced dramatically since this photo, taken in 1936Proof of a warming planetThe retreat of Papua's glaciers is driven by the same forces affecting ice around the world, Šabacká notes, a warming atmosphere caused by human activity, including the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas.As temperatures rise, the freezing point moves higher up mountains, so more precipitation falls as rain instead of snow, even in places that once saw regular snowfall.El Niño events can accelerate this process, while local factors such as cloud cover, snowfall and mountain topography influence its pace.The mountains in Papua are just 450km (280 miles) south of the equator, where "permanent ice can survive only at very high altitudes and within a narrow range of climatic conditions", Šabacká says.A small increase in temperature, a higher freezing point or shift from snowfall to rainfall can determine whether a glacier survives at all, she adds.The glaciers' retreat is evidence the Earth has been warming over a long period - and their disappearance "removes both a biological habitat and part of a culturally significant landscape".Image source, Marie ŠabackáImage caption, Šabacká, seen taking samples from Puncak Jaya, says Papua's vanishing glaciers are unique as they are so far from other glacier systemsA spiritual anchorAt least five groups of Indigenous people have had strong spiritual ties to Puncak Jaya for generations.The Moni people refer to it as Mbainggela, and believe their ancestors watch over the mountain. To the Amungme people, the range is known as Nemangkawi, or the "White Arrow"."Parents and grandparents prayed their children would have hearts like the White Arrow, never straying from the proper path," says Elfrida Natkime, a young Amungme woman. "It symbolises honesty, purity and moral integrity."According to traditional Amungme beliefs, Nemangkawi symbolises how people should live.Amungme environmental activist Adolfina Kum stresses how important the peak is to her people - and how traditions and cultural foundations risk being shattered as the ice melts."How would Muslims feel if Mecca were destroyed? How would Catholics feel if Rome or the Vatican were destroyed?" she asks. "For the Amungme people, that is what it feels like when Nemangkawi is destroyed."Image caption, The mountain holds immense spiritual significance for Indigenous people like Justinus, a man from the Moni tribeFor many Indigenous Papuans, the disappearance of the glacier is not an isolated event.The discovery of vast copper and gold deposits transformed the region during the 20th Century, and the development of extractive industrial projects have reshaped parts of the landscape.Entire mountain faces have been excavated and roads, industrial infrastructure and settlements have transformed surrounding valleys.Papuans say the development has brought jobs, roads, education and economic opportunities, but also environmental degradation and decades of social conflict. Some have lost access to their ancestral lands as mining expanded. The BBC has approached Freeport, which operates Papua's Grasberg mine, one of the world's largest gold and copper operations, for comment."Every time I see the mountains, I feel amazed, but I also feel sadness," says Elfrida Natkime. "Since the company came, I have seen the exploitation. But the development has also provided a livelihood for many people."Image source, Project Pressure/Klaus ThymannImage caption, This 3D rendition by Klaus Thymann's Project Pressure shows ice coverage at the date of capture in 2025As local communities watch their sacred landscapes change, scientists and explorers are racing to document what is left.Using drones and three-dimensional mapping techniques, Danish researcher Klaus Thymann and his team have created a detailed model of what remains.From the early 2000s to 2025, the glaciated area has receded by 95%, he says. "There's almost no ice left. Those are the facts."Thymann says glaciers are "incredibly powerful" as indicators of climate change."When people hear that something described as 'eternal' is disappearing, it triggers a reaction," he explains.Adolfina Kum believes communities "lose an important source of strength" when sacred mountains, forests or ancestral places are disturbed."I often describe it as pulling out the roots of a tree. Once the roots are removed, the tree loses its foundation."

schema.headline: Indonesia Carstensz Pyramid: Papua's 'eternal snow' on Puncak Jaya is about to disappear forever

title: Israel v Republic of Ireland: Republic of Ireland to wear black armbands for Israel game
description: Republic of Ireland players intend to wear black armbands "in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict" for Sunday's Nations League game a
body: Republic of Ireland players intend to wear black armbands "in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict" for Sunday's Nations League game against Israel in Hungary, after confirming they will go ahead with the fixture.Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell confirmed one player has withdrawn from the squad before the match.But he added that a vote among the squad produced a "significant majority" in favour of playing.As well as the intention to wear black armbands for Sunday's 'away' game against Israel in Debrecen, Courell said the players will make further gestures for the initial game and the return 'home' fixture against Israel next Sunday in Serbia.The fixtures have been embroiled in controversy since the two teams were drawn to play each other in Group B3.Republic of Ireland players faced calls to withdraw from the games because of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war with a "Stop The Game" campaign - organised by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine - gathering pace."One of their requests is to remove their media obligations for the remainder of this window," Courell said at Saturday's delayed news conference."They also have the intention to wear black armbands in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict. "There will be elements of the pre-match ceremony not be partaken in by the Republic of Ireland and it is also the intention of the players to make a significant contribution to charitable donation by virtue of both [Israel] match fees and also the fixture against Austria at the Aviva [Stadium in Dublin on Thursday]."There appeared to be real doubt on Saturday morning whether the fixture would take place.A pre-match news conference with manager Heimir Hallgrimsson and a player, scheduled for 09:15 BST, was postponed just 15 minutes before it was scheduled to start, with reporters informed it would instead take place after the team's training session which was also delayed.The players were locked in a meeting back at their hotel after it emerged a player, believed to be goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, withdrew from the game in protest with several other expressing their concerns about fielding.Around 13:00 BST, players began to filter out of the meeting room, with it then confirmed the news conference would indeed go ahead, back at Nagyerdei Stadion at 14:30, with training to follow.More than five hours after the initial news conference was scheduled to begin, Courell - flanked by Hallgrimsson and FAI director of football John Martin - confirmed a players' vote passed by a "significant majority" to play the game."This morning, a player expressed their discomfort at the fixture and indicated their intent to withdraw," Courell said."This new variable required time for the rest of the squad to consider and what proceeded was another four hours of conversations, predominantly among the players, but also at times with coaching staff and the [FAI] executive."There were a lot of positions presented and the association is fully respectful of everyone's right to their respective opinion."Former Republic of Ireland manager Brian Kerr and ex-international James McClean are among those to have backed calls for a boycott of the fixtures.The armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.Hallgrimsson relayed that nobody "can understand the pressure that has been going on these players" and said the lengthy meeting on Saturday stemmed from "a change of mind for one of the players to play the game"."All of the rest of the players are training today," he confirmed."The balance [to play] changed with this [withdrawal] and obviously it was an ongoing discussion but we came to a conclusion and the game is going ahead."We will train and there will probably be more discussions tonight and probably tomorrow. It's a unique situation and we are just trying to limit the damage."The Republic of Ireland lost their opening Nations League fixture in Kosovo on Thursday, a match overshadowed in the build-up by the Israel games.Asked whether the far from ideal preparation for Sunday's game would affect the players, the Irish boss said "we will see"."Nobody is comfortable but it's about limiting the damage, both personally and for Irish football, that we need to find some solution on it," Hallgrimsson added."There is no action we do that everyone will agree to, so we need to find a solution to limit the damage for us as a group, for Ireland as a nation and the association for football in Ireland."We don't know the consequences if we don't play the game but a lot of players share a common feeling, so there are two choices and both are tough. It's a situation you can't win."

schema.headline: Israel v Republic of Ireland: Republic of Ireland to wear black armbands for Israel game

title: 'It's a brutal adjustment': How to cope when your child goes to university
description: Your child has left home. Here's why it's time to stop checking up on themImage source, Getty ImagesByKirstie BrewerBBC NewsLuke felt overwhelmed with
body: Your child has left home. Here's why it's time to stop checking up on themImage source, Getty ImagesByKirstie BrewerBBC NewsLuke felt overwhelmed with both pride and grief after dropping his son off at university for the first time."It feels like a brutal adjustment," he says."After 18 years of seeing him every day and taking care of him, I miss him so much and I don't really know what to do with myself."Like other parents we have spoken to, Luke (not his real name) and his wife have felt compelled to regularly check a Facebook group for parents and carers with children living in the same halls of residence, as well as a university-wide version with more than 2,000 members.At first, being in these groups felt helpful for practical information, particularly in the weeks before his son headed to university, Luke says. But now they're feeding his anxiety."People will post things like: 'Is it normal to spend so much time in your room?'; 'I'm worried my daughter is struggling to make friends'; 'My child isn't replying to messages - how often are people hearing from theirs?'"There have also been questions about Amazon parcel logistics, requests to borrow cereal bowls and what tog duvet other people's children were given.Luke thinks these kinds of social media groups have fuelled his temptation to keep checking his son's location on a tracking app "to make sure he is going out enough and finding friends".Because his messages and calls go largely unanswered, Luke will also watch videos posted on the university's social media accounts, hoping to catch a glimpse of his son among the throngs of Freshers. Other parents have sheepishly confessed they're doing the same.Across universities, some enterprising parents have set up the sort of WhatsApp group chats you'd more typically find being used when children are at school. Only rather than asking after lost jumpers and what day PE is, these groups might be used to try to parent long-distance.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Some parents say they feel compelled to regularly check a Facebook group for parents and carers"Sometimes parents send their child to university and they're not even worried, but then these group chats create a worry that something might be wrong," says Rayyah Uddin, 20, a third-year student at the University of Nottingham.She knows of WhatsApp group chats being set up by parents of first-year students at her university and has also seen parents use TikTok to share their worries about their child not making friends, and asking other parents for their help."These are issues the students should really be figuring out for themselves, and it is better if parents try and talk to their child rather than immediately jump to other parents," she says.Not hearing from your child all the time isn't necessarily a cause for concern - "they might just be having a really good time and are getting absorbed into university life," Rayyah adds.Parent social media groups can be useful, according to psychologist Charlotte Armitage, but not when they are used to share private difficulties, track movements or ask questions that the student is capable of asking themselves."Constant checking, tracking or intervening may soothe the parent in the short term, but it can inadvertently communicate to the young adult: 'I am not sure you can cope without me.'""Of course, where there is a credible safeguarding concern, a significant change in behaviour, or a known risk to their wellbeing, parents should act."'Students should be figuring it out for themselves'A big part of going to university is about being independent, says Manchester University student Archie Forde, 19, who has heard stories of parents "pinging phones at 3am and calling their kids 12 times a week".He thinks parents turning to social media groups have "mostly fair concerns" but are going about things in the wrong way.The groups can be "echo chambers where everyone just spins each other out about their kids", he says, and suggests having a proper conversation with your child about boundaries, before university starts.Every family will have different ideas about what is overbearing, but a student shouldn't have the worry of choosing between "cutting back parents' communication and ruining that relationship, or responding to a flurry of texts at pre-drinks and detaching yourself from the social situation".Image source, Archie FordeImage caption, Archie Forde, 19, says parents turning to social media groups are going about things in the wrong wayWriting a letter or sending a parcel - without the expectation of a getting a response - could be a good way to let your child know you're thinking of them, "without it feeling like a demand", says child psychologist Laverne Antrobus.Perhaps negotiate a time to check in with them, "and be prepared to not always have long conversations," she says.And when you do speak to your child, "make sure your curiosity is genuine, rather than half-informed by the surveillance you've been doing"."Already knowing where they've been and what they've been up to makes for an unrewarding conversation with them and children are bright - they will know."Rayyah says she looks forward to properly catching up when she goes home."If you've spent months being closely monitored it might feel as if you haven't really been away or gained any independence; it could feel frustrating."'I didn't know who I was without the kids'Having seen three children off to university, Nichola McClellan wants to reassure parents that it does get easier. Based in Cheshire, she shares her experience of being an "empty nester" on social media, external."It's a huge emotional adjustment after years of your life revolving around your children, so we need to give ourselves time and permission to miss them. "I think back to how lost I felt. I didn't know who I was without the kids. "They're learning how to leave," she says, "but we're learning how to let go."Rather than expect constant contact, Nichola sends "little no-pressure messages" on their family WhatsApp group."'Love you', 'proud of you' - things that don't require an answer."They have a proper catch-up roughly once a week, and she has learned not to take it personally if she doesn't hear from them."Sometimes that is a really good sign, it means they're getting on with this new life you've spent all those years preparing them for. "You don't stop being a parent when they leave home - but you do get the opportunity to rediscover parts of yourself that perhaps got a little lost along the way. There really is so much to look forward to."Three expert tips on letting go Psychologist Charlotte Armitage shares her advice to help parents cope with this new stage of parenthood: Think twice before you post on a parents' group Feeling anxious, bereft or excluded is normal, but those feelings don't always require action. Before posting on a group or stepping in, Armitage says ask yourself: "Is this a genuine safety issue? Have I given my young adult the chance to deal with it? Am I helping them become more capable, or managing my own anxiety?"Steer clear of constant checking and tracking or intervening These may soothe you in the short term, but can inadvertently communicate to your young adult: "I am not sure you can cope without me." Of course, parents should step in when there is a safeguarding concern or risk to their child's wellbeingThe most valuable message you can send To help your child settle into adult life, Armitage says the most valuable message you can send is: "I am here if you need me and I believe you can do this."Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues raised in this story?

schema.headline: 'It's a brutal adjustment': How to cope when your child goes to university

title: Why bookshops are booming in the TikTok age
description: Opening your own book shop might be a lofty daydream for some bookworms looking to escape their 9-5, but more and more people are making it a reality.
body: Opening your own book shop might be a lofty daydream for some bookworms looking to escape their 9-5, but more and more people are making it a reality.According to the Booksellers Association, the number of independent book shops in the UK and Ireland is now at its highest level since 2012, with 1,086 stores in 2025 - up from a record low of 867 in 2016.But what is the reality of life as a small bookseller, competing with Amazon, finding new customers, and actually trying to make a profit?Sally Flint, 57, opened The Book Stop in Brigg, North Lincolnshire, just six weeks ago.So far, the "dream" move is living up to her expectations, but it has not been without its challenges. "It's brilliant. It's just like it's Christmas Day every day, because you're just with other people who love books and love reading," she says.However, to make her dream possible, Sally is working up to 14 hours a day.She describes her first foray into bookselling as a "steep learning curve", but says she is having "lots of fun along the way".

schema.headline: Why bookshops are booming in the TikTok age

title: Murder or medical mix-up? New questions in the Colin Norris case
description: The podcast series comes a week after a public inquiry reported on the case of former neonatal nurse Lucy Letby who was convicted of murdering seven b
body: The podcast series comes a week after a public inquiry reported on the case of former neonatal nurse Lucy Letby who was convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others at a hospital in Chester a decade ago. While the circumstances are very different, Norris' supporters also argue that his case hinges on disputed interpretations of medical evidence.The story begins in 2002 when Norris, a 26-year-old nurse, originally from Glasgow, found Ethel in an hypoglycemic coma as she recovered from a broken hip.Doctors took blood samples to find out what caused her blood sugar to drop so low. The test results seemed conclusive - she had a massive amount of insulin in her blood. She died 21 days later, sparking a murder investigation.A nurse who had been on shift on the night Ethel was found told the police that Norris had predicted the 86-year-old might not last the night. He quickly became the prime suspect.The police operation trawled retrospectively through all the deaths on Norris's wards, looking for potential murders that may have gone unnoticed.They identified three other cases of unexplained severe hypoglycemic deaths and one where the patient recovered.No blood tests had been taken from these cases at the time of their deaths to be able to prove insulin poisoning but experts for the prosecution said in court that their medical charts showed persistent and severe low blood sugar readings.They said that because this was so rare in non-diabetics that it must be murder.When it came to court in 2007, experts called by the defence said four of the five patients had died of natural causes.But after a five-month trial and a deadlocked jury, Norris was convicted by a majority of 11-1 and told he would not be eligible for parole for 30 years.After the verdict, Ethel's son Stuart Hall said: "I don't think he should come out again. He's got the knowledge to commit murder but do it discreetly."When I got involved in the case in 2009, Norris, who is now known as Colin Campbell, had just lost his first appeal against conviction.Two years later, new scientific evidence came to light which challenged one of the key assumptions underpinning the prosecution case. It claimed hypoglycemia - low blood sugar - in the frail and elderly is not as vanishingly rare as was once thought, suggesting the jury had been misinformed.This new evidence was submitted for a second appeal, which took another 14 years to be heard.During that appeal last year, experts for Norris argued that the symptoms seen in several of the patients could occur naturally in elderly, frail people.Experts for the Crown maintained the deaths were medically distinct.They said their blood sugar readings were refractory, meaning they kept coming back despite being given glucose, whereas naturally-occurring hypoglycemia can be easily corrected with a treatment such as a sugary drink.They argued this distinction could only be explained by deliberate insulin poisoning.Were the syringes accidentally switched?Initially, we discounted this scenario because we assumed medical staff would be alerted if a diabetic patient had accidentally been given dextrose instead of insulin.  However, endocrinologist Prof Joel Zonszein, an expert in diabetes, said the amount given would not have caused a severe illness."The answer is very different from somebody getting insulin," he said. "Insulin is much more aggressive. Giving too much sugar does not cause a coma and it will take more that 24 hours until the person goes into a coma. It's completely different."Prof Zonszein also said the amount of insulin Ethel may have been given accidentally would have produced the high readings in her immunoassay blood test taken five hours later.He said the drip of dextrose would have masked the insulin, making it harder to notice, but the blood test result would still register a very high level of insulin.If the syringes were accidentally switched, is that a mix-up rather than a murder?That still leaves another question: what caused Ethel to fall into a coma in the first place?Our investigation found all five patients had been prescribed medications, all were on antibiotics and two of the women were on powerful painkillers.All of these are known to increase the risk of severe hypoglycaemia in frail, elderly patients.It is possible that a strong opioid prescribed to Ethel for her post-op pain put her in a coma, and insulin meant for somebody else was accidentally given to her before the blood sample, which proved poisoning, was taken.The Court of Appeal ruled last year on whether naturally-occurring hypoglycaemia could explain the medical collapse of the four patients beyond Ethel Hall but ruled the case put by Norris' team got nowhere close to undermining the safety of his convictions and rejected the appeal on all grounds.They also rejected Norris' lawyers' attempts to go to the Supreme Court. An application has been made to the European Court of Human Rights, by Norris' lawyers, but solicitor Rory Hearty says this "hurdle" will take many years.

schema.headline: Murder or medical mix-up? New questions in the Colin Norris case

title: Meet the pensioners spending the kids' inheritance
description: Happily retired, Sarah Moorhouse is using her private pension "to go places and do nice things at the drop of a hat".While other retirees with a decen
body: Happily retired, Sarah Moorhouse is using her private pension "to go places and do nice things at the drop of a hat".While other retirees with a decent monthly pension income may choose to build up an inheritance for their children, Sarah, 64, and her husband Geoff are opting to spend their money on living life to the max."We like going to Scotland," says Sarah, a retired school administrator. "We've been down to Cambridgeshire, which was lovely. We go up to the Lake District quite regularly to a holiday cottage, and we're planning to go to Norfolk."The couple, who live in the Yorkshire Dales, go on holiday four or five times a year, spending hundreds of pounds each time because, in Sarah's view, "you only have one opportunity at life". They did recently sell their vintage Sunbeam Alpine sports car. But only so they could replace it with a more modern, sporty two-seater convertible, a Mazda MX-5."I'm of an age where I'm going to friends' and acquaintances' funerals, and I think you just need to live life and enjoy it while you can, because it's a very precious commodity," says Sarah.Sarah and Geoff are part of a global personal finance phenomenon that has been dubbed "skiing", which stands for spending the kids' inheritance. It is challenging the notion that assets will get handed down to the next generation.One in seven UK parents of children of all ages (15%) now plan to prioritise enjoying their money in their retirement over leaving an inheritance, according to a March report, external by pension provider Standard Life. And in the US, the number of people expecting to get an inheritance from their parents dropped to 20% last year, from 25% in 2024, according to a study, external by financial services firm Northwestern Mutual. Sarah and Geoff have two adult daughters. One of them, Poppy, tells the BBC that she couldn't be happier that her parents are out and about having fun.She firmly rejects the notion that she and her sister should expect an inheritance. "To me that's wild. It never even crossed my mind that I'll get money when my mum and dad die. I'd so much rather them do what they want to do."Mike Ambery, retirement and savings director at Standard Life, believes that the move towards skiing in the UK has been driven by the disappearance of final-salary pensions, which provide guaranteed monthly pension payments that last for as long as the retiree lives.Instead, more people in the UK now have what are called defined contribution pension pots, which can run out. Ambery argues that it's easier to be generous with a legacy if you know your retirement income will last as long as you need it.He also points to pensioners wanting to simply enjoy themselves after a life of working. "It's just having a little bit of indulgence to enjoy life. Let's face it, working life can be very hard for some people."Not all retirees are well off, of course. In the UK, 16% of pensioners live in poverty, , externalaccording to the Joseph Rowntree Foundation charity. The figure for the US is 15.4%, newly released data shows., externalBut at the same time, UK pensioners have seen their disposable income, excluding housing costs, increase by more than that of non-pensioners over the last three decades, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies think tank, external.Originally from Berkshire, Karen has lived in Provence in the south of France for the past 11 years, and spends more than £10,000 a year on holidays."This year, I'm going to a yoga retreat. I did one in March in Morocco," she says. "Then in October into November I'm going to Vietnam and Laos to do a little bit of a tour."She describes herself as semi-retired, as she tops up her private pension by still doing some business consultancy work, the job she used to do full-time.When it comes to how much money she has per month, she says that her income is the same as when she was working full-time. In addition to her pension and income from her part-time work, she gains 40% of her funds from renting out a property.But Karen insists she's not "crazy with money" and likes "to get a deal".Like Sarah Moorhouse she won't get her UK state pension until she is 67. That's currently a standard £12,547.60 a year for people who reached the state pension age after April 2016, but it is due to go up next year.As a comparison, retirees in the US get state payments known as social security retirement benefits. The maximum annual amount starting from the "full retirement age" of 67 is $49,824 (£36,993)., external However, people can choose to take a lower payment, external from the age of 62.Matthew Loveless, a vice president at Northwestern Mutual, based in Ohio, says retirees need to be upfront with their adult children, some of whom might be expecting an inheritance that they intend to rely on.Back in Yorkshire, Sarah says that despite the spending, she has every intention of leaving her kids something. In the meantime she is planning her next holiday. "I've worked hard all my life and I think I deserve to have a bit of free time and to be able to do nice things."Additional reporting by Miguel Roca-Terry

schema.headline: Meet the pensioners spending the kids' inheritance

title: Keep dancing: 100-year-old leads Worcester charity flash mob
description: A 100-year-old man, already known for his dance moves through social media, led a flash mob with hundreds of people joining in.Wearing a bright red sh
body: A 100-year-old man, already known for his dance moves through social media, led a flash mob with hundreds of people joining in.Wearing a bright red shirt, Bernard Gilbert directed a dance to song King of the Road by country singer Roger Miller in Worcester city centre, with crowds erupting in applause after he finished.The former dance teacher previously went viral on social media for his moves at Fernhill House Care Home where he lives. His videos were seen more than 1.5m times."I love the dancing, once I get on the floor I forget everything, I just concentrate on what I'm doing," he said when the BBC interviewed him in June. The flash mob in Cathedral Square featured Got2Sing choir members as well as residents as they raised money for Alzheimer's Research UK. They learnt four dances, practised hard and rehearsed at home to prepare for the event, Fernhill House Care Home said."What an inspiring day, what a community, what a fantastic memory we've created together," it added.Organisers of Got2Sing Worcester described the flash mob as a "joyful afternoon" with singers "bringing their energy and talent" to the city centre."When a 100-year-old local legend leads the line dancing, you know it's going to be a good afternoon," they said.

schema.headline: Keep dancing: 100-year-old leads Worcester charity flash mob

title: Drumcree parade is challenged in High Court by residents' group
description: Drumcree parade: Judge urges parties to reach agreement and 'step back from the abyss'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The parade (pictured ab
body: Drumcree parade: Judge urges parties to reach agreement and 'step back from the abyss'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The parade (pictured above in 2018 on a 20th anniversary protest) will be allowed to march on the Garvaghy Road on Sunday ByMichael Fitzpatrick and Catherine DoyleBBC News NIUpdated 48 minutes agoA judge hearing the legal challenge to the Parades Commission's decision to allow the Orange Order to march on the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road in Portadown has given the parties involved a final opportunity to "reach an agreement" and "step back from the abyss.".Judge Patricia Smyth said the issue the court is dealing with is of "fundamental importance" to the entire society in Northern Ireland.She has adjourned the judicial review hearing for a short period to allow the Garvaghy Roads Residents Coaliton, the Orange Order and the Parades Commission to consider her plea.The commission on Friday announced that the parade can proceed on Sunday, for the first time in almost 30 years, with restrictions in place.The coalition has also applied to the Parades Commission for a protest to the walk on Sunday, listing the number of participants at 5,000. A decision is expected on Saturday, according to the commission. , externalRather than start at 13:00 BST on Sunday as intended, the commission has said the march can depart no later than 08:00 and with 35 participants rather than the 60 the Orange Order requested. No bands or supporters are allowed.The decision is facing the legal challenge from the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition, which opposes the march.On Saturday, a lawyer for the residents told the High Court it was unclear whether the Police Service of Northern Ireland's (PSNI) assessment referred to in the determination, was the "entirety" of what the police told the Parades Commission.Their legal team has asked for the full PSNI assessment as well as past assessments in order to see whether there had been any changes.Counsel for the residents said there had been a "significant change" in the Parades Commission's approach.Before adjourning the proceedings, Judge Patricia Smyth told the parties involved she would like to hear from them on a way forward in the short amount of time that was available.'Sense of shock'According to the Drumcree Catholic Church parish website, external, Mass takes place at 08:30 on Sundays in the church of St John the Baptist on the Garvaghy Road. When asked by BBC News NI if Mass time had been taken into consideration in their determination, the Parades Commission said commissioners "recognise that the timings set out in the determination" should allow the church service "to proceed as normal".Image source, Catholic Communications Office archiveImage caption, Archbishop Martin said his thoughts were with those affected by the situation In a statement issued on Saturday afternoon, the leader of the Catholic Church in Ireland, Archbishop Eamon Martin, called for "prayers and support for a peaceful resolution to complex Garvaghy Road situation".He said he shares the "sense of shock and disappointment of so many people at recent developments".The archbishop added his thoughts were with those who this situation brings "back deeply traumatic and painful memories"."I also appeal for support for the patient use of solely lawful and democratic processes to resolve this deeply complex and emotive situation."'March going to clash with parishioners'Fr Peter Clarke, from St John the Baptist, said he is concerned the march is "going to clash" with parishioners coming and going from the church. Following Friday's determination, the priest said he emailed the commission to express his concerns and stated he "doesn't know how they came to" their conclusion, which is now "out of their hands".Fr Clarke said he has "unhappy recollections" of the Drumcree dispute during the 1990s and "wouldn't like to see" a return to those days.Parishioners at St Patrick's Church on William Street are also likely to be affected ahead of the 10:00 service, according to the priest.He added "tensions are high" in the community, and said he will be addressing the situation during Sunday's service.'Orange Order will comply full with the law'Image caption, Nigel Dawson, Portadown District Master, says he hopes the parade can pass peacefullyIn a statement issued on Saturday, the Portadown District Orange Order branch said while they were "not happy" with further restrictions to their parade, they would "comply fully with the law and determination"."We now ask our community to do likewise. We would appeal to everyone to conduct themselves responsibly and peacefully and not to do anything that could increase tensions within the community," District Master Nigel Dawson said.Dawson added the lodge had followed the commissions determinations for 28 years and "all we ask now is that same respect" is shown by those affected by this decision.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The decision is facing the legal challenge from the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition, pictured arriving to court with their legal teamIn the Parade Commission's determination, which was published on Friday afternoon,, external it said it had received "various written and oral submissions" from organisers, residents, police, political parties, church representatives and others."This decision is not, and should not be perceived, as a victory for one side or a loss for another," the determination also stated.The Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition lodged a judicial review after the commission gave the Orange Order permission to march on Garvaghy Road.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The Parades Commission has determined that the parade can depart Drumcree Parish Church no later than 08:00 BST on SundaySpeaking on his way into court, Breandán Mac Cionnaith, from the coalition, said they were going to court "to convince the law to see sense"."We are here to seek justice for our community in Portadown."On Friday, group said they were ''furious'' over the decision, adding that the community were "fearful about what will happen over the weekend".Elected representatives from Sinn Féin and the Social Democratic Labour Party (SDLP) were among the crowd outside the court on Saturday morning.Image source, PacemakerImage caption, Breandán Mac Cionnaith, from the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition, gathered with others outside the High Court in Belfast on Friday The five-person commission, led by Prof Evelyn Collins, held face-to-face talks with the Orange Order earlier this week, and held a separate meeting with the residents' coalition.Senior police officers were also consulted about the planned parade.Within the 31-paragraph determination by the Parades Commission, details were revealed of conversations held with the PSNI.The document stated: "The police made both written and oral submissions, indicating that they, at the time of making them, had no information indicating that the parade would result in disorder or violence."The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) said it had activated "mutual aid arrangements to support contingency planning for a policing operation" in Portadown on Sunday.It is understood about 200 officers are coming from Scotland.Image source, Pacemaker PressImage caption, Unionist representative Jamie Bryson and Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) members Carla Lockhart MP, Diane Dodds MLA and Alderman Dean McCullough pictured arriving to court on Saturday morningOn Friday, DUP MP Carla Lockhart said residents have "nothing to fear" and asked them not to get "caught up in hysteria"."Thirty-five men walking down a road silently with no bands in an orderly fashion."These men work, live and do business in this community," she added.She said Sinn Féin should "show political leadership and ensure calm remains across the community".Drumcree Then and Now: Part 2The State of Us The Parades Commission has given the Garvaghy Road march the go ahead after 28 years. Tara Mills and Declan Harvey explore the arguments that tipped the scale.However Sinn Féin President Mary-Lou McDonald said the decision to allow the parade was "utterly reckless" adding that it shows a "complete disregard" for the rights of the community of the Garvaghy road."This is a grave situation, recklessness of this scale of course has implications and consequences," she said.She called for anyone that can intervene, including the prime minister and taoiseach, to "put this right".When did the Drumcree dispute begin?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, British soldiers erect a security fence at Drumcree Church in July 2002The Parades Commission has been in the political spotlight since its previous Drumcree determination was quashed in the High Court in August.A review of the commission has since been ordered by the Northern Ireland Office.The Drumcree parade dispute began in the mid-1990s and it almost derailed the peace process at the time.Violence related to the dispute resulted in riots, roadblocks and murders.When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995 there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years.The Parades Commission began operating in 1998 to regulate parades and try to defuse tension around marches.Its decision not to allow a march down the Garvaghy Road that summer has been challenged by the order over the past three decades.

schema.headline: Drumcree parade is challenged in High Court by residents' group

title: Manchester City charges: Could club be stripped of eight trophies?
description: It is one of the biggest talking points from the Manchester City case. Should City be stripped of the eight trophies they won between 2009 and 2018, t
body: It is one of the biggest talking points from the Manchester City case. Should City be stripped of the eight trophies they won between 2009 and 2018, the period in which they were accused of breaking Premier League financial rules?Judging by social media, many fans of rival clubs are now hoping for such an outcome. However BBC Sport has been told there has been little appetite from within the Premier League - both the organisation and clubs - for past titles to be stripped from CityDoes that put an end to it?Not quite, as the decision will be made by an independent panel which is yet to hold a "sanction hearing". That means it cannot be ruled out, although a points deduction, huge fine or possibly even expulsion from the Premier League are thought to be more likely.Here, BBC Sport analyses this difficult issue and decision the panel is now facing."I think we still have a chance to win that league… and then they have to pay me the bonus and give me the medal."It was almost two years ago that Jose Mourinho mischievously raised the possibility that his former club Manchester United could be handed the 2018 Premier League title held by Manchester City.Under Mourinho, United finished second to City by 19 points in 2018, his final full campaign in charge at Old Trafford.City have always denied wrongdoing. But now we know they have been found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges, was Mourinho right? Premier League rules do not directly make reference to such a sanction, with a fine, points deduction or expulsion listed as possible punishments. However, they also allow for a disciplinary commission panel to impose a penalty "as it shall think fit". That theoretically could include retrospectively-applied points deductions, or the stripping of titles.Many will argue that if upheld after any appeal, the nature and scale of the wrongdoing City have been found guilty of warrants such as sanction on the basis that titles were won unfairly, and any misrepresentation of revenue and costs gave them a crucial competitive advantage.City were accused of a wide range of rule breaches, centred around claims that they inflated sponsorship revenue from connected companies and made other "off the books" payments to circumvent football's financial rules.So with a cloud hanging over the trophy-laden era City have enjoyed since the takeover of the club by Abu Dhabi billionaire Sheikh Mansour in 2008, could asterisks now be applied to the titles City won during the period in which they have been found to have broken the rules?Could they be left blank? Or, as implied by Mourinho, reallocated to those teams who finished runners-up to City?Those clubs are: Premier League2011-12: Manchester United2013-14: Liverpool2017-18: Manchester UnitedFA Cup2010-11: Stoke CityEFL Cup2013-14: Sunderland2015-16: Liverpool2017-18: ArsenalCommunity Shield2012-13 ChelseaSuch a move would threaten to open the proverbial can of worms, raising questions over other accomplishments. For instance, there is now scepticism towards the various trophies Chelsea won in the 2010s, after the club were found to have made a catalogue of secret payments to agents over transfers, between 2011 and 2018. Some will ask that if retrospective action is applied to City, should the same not happen to Chelsea?It is impossible to know exactly to what extent City benefited on the field from their rule breaches. And which players they may not have been able to afford if they had adhered to the regulations.And what about the period between December 2018 and February 2023, when City stand accused of a failure to co-operate with Premier League investigations? Should retrospective action be applied then too? Jurgen Klopp's Liverpool finished runners-up to Pep Guardiola's City twice during that time, by a single point in both 2019 and 2022. Last year, the German coach joked he would host a party in his garden if his former club were suddenly awarded those titles.Some will conclude that the rule breaches between 2009 and 2018 helped City to lay the foundations on which Guardiola built on to achieve so much success, culminating in the Treble triumph of 2023. Does that era come into scope? Where does it end?For some, the mass reallocation of titles over such a long period would risk making a mockery of Premier League history, jeopardising its reputation and commercial viability. Others would argue that some 17 years after the first alleged breach, and with City accused of distorting the competition over multiple seasons, serious damage has already been done to the league's standing.And while there is no Premier League precedent, such concerns have not prevented such punishments being applied before in football. Juventus had the Serie A titles they won in 2005 and 2006 revoked as a result of the Calciopoli match-fixing scandal - when five Italians teams were penalised for attempting to influence results by picking certain referees. The first title was left blank by authorities, with the second reallocated to Inter Milan.There is also a British precedent. Elgin City won the 1992-93 Highland League, but were later stripped of the title after having been found to have fielded ineligible players.There are examples in other sports too. In 2012, Lance Armstrong was stripped of his seven Tour de France titles by the UCI, cycling's governing body, for doping. And the reallocation of medals has become commonplace in athletics as a result of positive drugs tests that can emerge long after events have taken place.In cases such as City's, involving financial rule breaches, the argument for such a punishment is more complicated. Many will see it as unfair that players and fans unconnected to any rule breaches should suffer by losing titles.And with some suggesting that relations between the United Arab Emirates and the UK could be put under serious pressure by this ruling, one can only imagine the diplomatic tensions if past titles were then taken away from the club. On Friday, former City midfielder Rodri dismissed talk of the club being stripped of some of the titles they won."What we did, they cannot take out of us," he added."It's something that is not paid by money. It's paid with effort, with the damage, with, you know, being shoulder to shoulder every day."I can tell you that everything was deserved, and I'm glad that I could live one of the best eras of English football in here."Others, however, will insist the rewriting of history is the only way of restoring the competition's official record, and rewarding clubs that competed within the rules.In terms of retrospective action, the compensation claims for lost earnings that several clubs are known to be considering launching against City are more likely than the stripping of titles. A lawyer told me: "The question isn't whether the clubs can take legal action... it's: Where does the line of people who have a case actually end?"The clubs who didn't win/qualify/stay up; the players who didn't get bonuses, contract extensions; the staff who missed out on bonuses; the agents who didn't get their uplift on their player deals..."It's endless and potentially so destructive to the whole ecosystem."Whatever happens, more division and disruption seems guaranteed.

schema.headline: Manchester City charges: Could club be stripped of eight trophies?

title: Manchester City charges: Khaldoon Al Mubarak confident club will prove innocence
description: Figure caption, Kieran Maguire on potential sanctions for Man CityByPaul BattisonBBC Sport Journalist and Ffion WynneBBC Sport JournalistUpdated 22 mi
body: Figure caption, Kieran Maguire on potential sanctions for Man CityByPaul BattisonBBC Sport Journalist and Ffion WynneBBC Sport JournalistUpdated 22 minutes agoManchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak says he is still confident of proving the club's innocence after they were found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules.City were accused of a wide range of rule breaches, centring around claims they inflated sponsorship revenue from connected companies and made other "off the books" payments to circumvent financial regulations.On Friday, it was announced City had been found guilty of the vast majority of the 115 charges brought against them and Al Mubarak has responded with a letter to fans on the club's website. "Following Friday's media reporting, many of you will have spent your evening answering questions and responding to messages from friends, family and colleagues. So have I," Al Mubarak said."Here's what I said to my family: The Premier League process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the club's innocence is just as strong as when this began."There are so many things that I would like to be able to share with you to help you understand why we feel so confident in our position. "But the strict confidentiality of the legal process and our determination to respect it means I cannot do that at the moment. Even this letter underwent several legal checks to make sure it complies."Premier League clubs are seeking legal advice about compensation relating to the charges, while BBC Sport has been told City will appeal.Sanctions on the club are yet to be announced, but repercussions could include a points deduction, expulsion from the Premier League or a huge fine. Al Mubarak, who was appointed as City's chairman after their 2008 takeover, also said his club was being "undermined". "While some people have been quick to reach their own conclusions, and there is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed," he added."There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club. We will not give them that opportunity."Meanwhile, Christian Purslow, a former Liverpool managing director and Aston Villa chief executive, who also held a senior role at Chelsea, said the City case could begin a chain of events that would be "appalling for the game".Speaking on Radio 4's Today programme, Purslow appeared alongside football law expert Paul Gilroy KC, who described the case as a "seismic moment for world football".Purslow said: "It's a sort of 'where does this end?' because if you look at every single season - the nine seasons which we now know Manchester City breached rules - then all of their 19 Premier League rivals in that season, to differing extents, suffered easy-to-compute loss. Whether it was a place in the Premier League - every place was worth £3m."Teams that came fifth who didn't make the Champions League maybe lost tens of millions of pounds - and of course teams that were relegated. Let's say the team that finished 18th would've finished 17th if Manchester City weren't there. And they, of course, suffered huge loss."If you add all those claims up, over nine years, and that's just in the Premier League, you can see that the potential here for this to spiral out of control is huge."Gilroy added that, so far, four clubs have put in protective claims "reserving the right to claim compensation if City are found guilty".'Very unsettling for football fans'The news, broken by the Athletic,, external came 1,327 days after City were charged by the Premier League in February 2023 following a four-year investigation, and 22 months after a hearing by an independent commission concluded.No official announcement has been made by the Premier League, which has declined to comment.Manchester City declined to comment on whether they had been found guilty, instead providing a statement which read: "Premier League process remains ongoing with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality."The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence."Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has urged the Premier League to come to a quick resolution.She told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I think most football fans will be feeling that this is not a good moment for football as a whole and I think Manchester City fans will be feeling very, very anxious about what happens next."It's very unsettling for football fans and I hope that it can be resolved as swiftly as possible."I will obviously look very closely as what comes out of this but we can't apply those rules for the Premier League. They have got to do it themselves and are going to have to resolve this as swiftly as possible - not just for the sake of Manchester City but for the sake of football."Figure caption, What do Man City charges mean and what happens next?Former chairman Bernstein feels 'absolutely awful'City won eight trophies in the period covered by the case, including three Premier League titles, three EFL Cups, one Community Shield and one FA Cup.The charges cover the managerial tenures of Roberto Mancini and Manuel Pellegrini, and the first two years under Pep Guardiola, who left the club at the end of last season after 10 years in charge.David Bernstein, who was Manchester City chairman from 1998-2003, told Times Radio he felt "absolutely awful" on hearing the news of City being found guilty - but admitted any punishment would have to be "more drastic" than a fine. "To see all this tarnished in this way is very sad," he said."I feel particularly bad for the wonderful supporters of the club who've stayed with the club through thick and thin."This whole process has taken too long already. So the appeal process now has to be done quickly because you've got the club playing with this cloud over its head and it's just not viable."The appeal process cannot go on for year after year, I think that would be a disaster, not just for this particular case but for English football generally. The timing is crucial."He continued: "I can't give a view on the punishment. If they are found, after the appeal, guilty of 115 charges, my beloved club is going to face a very severe penalty."All I would say is that money is not sufficient, it would have to be something, unfortunately, more drastic than that."Meanwhile, singer-songwriter Noel Gallagher says he is "shocked" at the news and it is "quite sad" for players and fans."A little surprised when I heard it on the radio. Surprised because the club have assured us all along that they vehemently denied any of these charges," the Oasis star and City fan said on the Let Me Talk podcast."So it was a bit of a shock to find out that we've been found guilty. But really overall just quite sad really. Sad for the fans and for the players."Follow Manchester City on BBC SoundsPre-match, post-match and topical City contentSubscribe and listen for everything you love about City

schema.headline: Manchester City charges: Khaldoon Al Mubarak confident club will prove innocence
